NEW YORK, Oct 29 : Chip stocks took another hit after Thursday's weak quarterly earnings report from Intel, which could make for interesting dynamics when trading reopens on Friday. The semiconductor index sold off in post-close trading on Thursday after chipmaker Intel blamed "near term headwinds across the PC industry," sending its shares tumbling 18 per cent in the after-hours session. That followed the SOX's 1.4 per cent drop during the regular session due to a messy earnings report from big AI spender Alphabet on Wednesday. Intel said a factory explosion in Israel will cost it roughly $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters because it has been shut down for about two weeks. Intel's fall took other big chip stocks down in post-close trading as well.  "Overall semis weakness after hours is primarily a function of INTC guide and negative sentiment spillover," said Michael James, equity sales trader at Rosenblatt Securities.

Intel's problems in the PC sector, an area of technology that does not garner the same scrutiny on Wall Street as the AI buildout, does not seem to necessarily mean big problems for other chipmakers that operate more prominently in AI. Nevertheless, investors in the less-active post-market trade chose to shoot first and ask questions later. AMD dropped 4 per cent and Broadcom fell 2 per cent. Among the biggest losers in the volatile session were the Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull ETF, which offers investors three times the daily performance of the SOX and was off 9 per cent. "The revenues missed due to lower PC demand and forward guidance also disappointed. As Google learned today, earnings matter," said Kim Caughey Forrest, founder and chief investment officer at Bokeh Capital Partners LLC. Google parent Alphabet dropped 13 per cent on Thursday. The SOX has been one of 2026's standout performers, rising more than 60 per cent as shortages of chips and equipment needed for the AI buildout drive up prices and profits at firms ranging from giant Nvidia and memory chip firm Micron to Marvell Technology.  But the momentum of that trade has been tested over the past month by tightening financing terms. That has kept some expected IPOs on the sidelines and put some highly leveraged AI infrastructure firms under pressure. The SOX has declined 13 per cent since hitting its recent high in October and is off 21 per cent from its all-time high in June.  That said, pre- and after-market trading often exaggerates moves relative to those in the more liquid regular session, particularly for stocks affected by a rival's news.  "I think it should not have much of an effect on the market," said Caughey Forrest. "It sounds like it was a PC issue. AMD may be a target for selling tomorrow too. Intel does not have much to do with AI, which is why the market might ignore it."

Source: Reuters

TOKYO, Oct 30 : The Bank of Japan is set to keep interest rates steady on Friday but stress its focus on preventing underlying inflation from overshooting its 2 per cent target, suggesting scope to hike borrowing costs as soon as December. Such guidance would reinforce the central bank's message last month that it has entered a new, more hawkish policy phase and is open to raising rates once every few months, analysts said. The pivot would also align the BOJ with its US and European counterparts eyeing near-term rate hikes to battle inflationary risks from the AI boom and the Iran war-induced energy shock. "Global price pressures from AI investment are quite strong, which means the recent inflation is partly demand driven," said Kazuo Momma, a former BOJ executive who is currently executive economist at Mizuho Research Institute.

"By declaring that its policy phase has changed, the BOJ is essentially telling markets it will hike rates once a quarter," he said, predicting rate hikes in December and March next year. At the two-day meeting ending on Friday, the BOJ is set to maintain its policy rate at 1.25 per cent, forgoing a back-to-back hike to spend more time scrutinising the effect of past rate hikes on lending conditions. In a quarterly report, the BOJ is likely to slightly revise up next fiscal year's price forecast and signal that underlying inflation has roughly achieved its 2 per cent target, people familiar with the matter have told Reuters. With wage gains becoming embedded and inflation expectations hovering around 2 per cent, the central bank will likely stress that it will now focus on anchoring inflation around its target by raising rates toward levels deemed neutral to the economy. Markets will scrutinise comments from Governor Kazuo Ueda's post-meeting news conference for hints on the pace and timing of further rate hikes. "If the BOJ were to say underlying inflation reached levels consistent with its 2 per cent price target, that would have important policy implications," said former BOJ official Nobuyasu Atago, who is currently chief economist at Rakuten Securities Economic Research Institute. "It would be a show of resolve the BOJ won't tolerate any further overshoot in inflation," and signal the chance of more nimble rate hikes next year, he said. With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised rates in September after delivering a hike in June - a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes in 2024 and 2025. Most analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise its policy rate to 1.5 per cent in December, followed by further hikes next year. Their terminal rate projection centres around 1.75 per cent to 2 per cent. Core consumer inflation exceeded the BOJ's 2 per cent target in September for the first time in nine months, as high fuel costs from the prolonged Middle East conflict blunt the impact of government fuel subsidies. In current quarterly projections made in July, the BOJ expects consumer inflation to accelerate in coming months as firms continue to pass on rising costs.

Oct 29 : Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase Global reported a quarterly profit on Thursday, snapping a three-quarter-long streak of losses, driven by lower operating expenses. Total operating expenses in the third quarter fell about 17 per cent to $1.15 billion, compared with $1.39 billion for the same period in the prior year. Cryptocurrency trading activity has struggled to regain momentum this year as investors grappled with shifting monetary policy expectations, weaker flows into digital asset investment products and periodic market volatility. Transaction revenue dropped 43 per cent to $590.2 million during the quarter, from $1.05 billion a year earlier. The company reported a profit of $718.7 million, or $2.51 per share, for the quarter ended September 30, compared with $432.6 million, or $1.50 per share, a year earlier.

Oct 29 : Reddit CEO Steve Huffman outlined a plan on Thursday to make signing-in mandatory for most content as the company grapples with data scraping and declining search referral traffic in recent months. Huffman warned that total daily active unique visitors (DAUq) could fall by a low double-digit percentage in the fourth quarter from about 130 million currently, if search referral traffic continues to decline further. Shares of the company fell more than 9 per cent in extended trading. Search engine referrals to Reddit decreased by more than one million on average each week during October, he said. In the US, its biggest market by revenue, DAUq fell 2 per cent to 50.7 million. Reddit, which licenses its data to OpenAI and Alphabet's Google, has sued IPO-bound Anthropic, Perplexity AI and three data scraping companies, accusing them of illegally collecting Reddit's data.

Oct 29 : Amazon.com on Thursday reported a massive cash burn in the third quarter and forecast holiday-quarter revenue largely below Wall Street estimates, sending shares lower. Investors soured on the company, driving shares down nearly 7 per cent in extended trading. The shares had declined 4.3 per cent in regular trading to end at $243.79. The Seattle-based retailer expects revenue of between $240.0 billion and $247.0 billion in the fourth quarter, compared with analysts' average estimate of $244.51 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. The company said it burned $42.4 billion on a trailing 12-month basis in the September quarter, driven by capital expenditure of $77.26 billion which was some $20 billion above estimates, according to data compiled by LSEG. Amazon reported cash burn of $7.6 billion in the prior quarter, and generated $14.8 billion in the third quarter of last year.

"The free cash flow looks like the ugly part of the report," said Dave Wagner, portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors. "Operations generated plenty of cash but their capex just absolutely swallowed it." "The trend is pretty steep and pretty negative, and that's the big thing that is alarming in this report." Like competitors, Amazon has made a huge spending commitment to developing AI software and infrastructure, forecasting $220 billion in capital expenditures this year. Amazon and Google parent Alphabet have maintained their spending expectations, though Microsoft on Wednesday lowered its own to $170 billion from $175 billion. Jesse Cohen, a senior analyst at Investing.com, also pointed to Amazon's free cash flow and "weak guidance" as reasons for the share decline. "Amazon's third-quarter report landed as a double disappointment." CLOUD BUSINESS DRIVES GROWTH Revenue at Amazon Web Services rose 39 per cent to $46 billion in the third quarter ended September, compared with analysts' estimate for a 38.2 per cent increase to $45.61 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. AWS revenue recorded a 37 per cent jump in the second quarter. The company also maintained its annual capital spending forecast of about $220 billion. Advertising sales were another disappointment, rising just 12 per cent to $19.6 billion from a year earlier, below the 18 per cent estimate from LSEG — the first time it missed analyst estimates in seven quarters. The results marked much slower growth than the second quarter's 26 per cent or the 2025 third quarter's 22 per cent. The downbeat fourth-quarter outlook signals US retailers could face pain in the holiday season, as consumers tighten shopping budgets amid higher gasoline prices and the rising cost of living. Still, recent industry forecasts predict holiday sales will accelerate from last year. The National Retail Federation earlier this month predicted a 4.2 per cent jump in total US holiday season sales. While retail sales account for the majority of Amazon's revenue, investor focus has shifted sharply toward its cloud computing business, Amazon Web Services, in recent years, as the tech company spends heavily to build out data centers and compete in the global AI race. Amazon's cloud unit grew at its fastest pace in nearly five years. At its e-commerce business, Amazon has been rolling out faster delivery services globally and expanding to more rural areas in the US to draw more shoppers.

Oct 29 : Intel shares plunged 14 per cent on Thursday after the chipmaker said a deadly explosion at its Israel factory would erase roughly $600 million in revenue over two quarters, with the full financial fallout still uncertain. The US chipmaker also warned of flagging PC revenue through the first half of next year, as exponential increases in memory prices have weighed on sales. If the stock were to lose this much ground in Friday's session, Intel would shed over $80 billion in market value. The gloomy outlook reverberated across the chip sector, sending Nvidia, Broadcom, AMD, Micron, Qualcomm and Arm Holdings' US-listed shares between 1 per cent and 6 per cent lower in extended trading. The October explosion at its Kiryat Gat, Israel factory, or fab, killed two and seriously injured one, according to local media reports. Finance chief David Zinsner said Intel planned to start ramping up production at the facility by the end of this week after a two-week shutdown.

The company said the fourth-quarter revenue outlook would be reduced by roughly $300 million and its gross margins by about 200 basis points, Zinsner said in an interview with Reuters. He said the company expects a similar revenue impact in the first quarter.  Intel is in the process of determining which wafers are salvageable for use and sale after the blast.  "We're still assessing all of the wafers to see which ones are usable and which ones aren't, so we'll have to see whether there is an impact that stretches beyond that," Zinsner said. The Kiryat Gat fab largely produces data center chips using the company's 10 nanometer manufacturing process. "The explosion at Kiryat Gat, one of Intel’s major manufacturing sites, is unfortunate and brought down Intel’s capacity," Hendi Susanto, portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds, said. "The question is whether Intel can build capacity fast enough to capture it." SLOWING PC SALES Intel's forecast could test investor confidence in a stock that has more than doubled this year, as investors weigh ongoing manufacturing constraints and soft PC demand against strong demand for its AI server chips and efforts to revive growth through a costly foundry expansion. Zinsner said he expects the PC slowdown will continue through the first half of next year. The company expects PC revenue to decline in the mid-twenty percentage range for its fourth quarter, Zinsner said in the interview. Sales in Intel's PC chip business fell 5 per cent to $8.10 billion, missing estimates of $8.98 billion. Investors have been watching for signs that demand has stabilized despite the company's expectation for a soft personal-computing market in the second half of this year and into 2027. "Client computing is still a big factor in Intel's earnings so while it is likely short-term, it will still impact earnings for the near term and I think that's the biggest issue," said Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy. The results also put a spotlight on Intel's funding plans. In August, the company raised $23 billion from an upsized share offering, as it seeks to challenge industry leaders such as TSMC in contract chip manufacturing.  Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion, below analysts' average estimate of $17.07 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. Adjusted profit is expected to be 25 cents per share, trailing estimates of 43 cents. WASHINGTON, Oct 29 : A meteorite found in 2022 in the Sahara in Mali formed in the Martian crust at least 4.1 billion years ago, according to scientists, making the reddish igneous rock perhaps the oldest of the 435 meteorites from Mars known on Earth. The researchers said the composition of the meteorite, called Teghaza 001, is providing insight into the environment early in the history of Earth's planetary neighbor, with fresh evidence of liquid water on the surface that bolsters the notion that primordial Mars may have been conducive to microbial life. Planetary scientist Yang Liu of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, which is managed by Caltech, called the meteorite "a witness to a time when Mars was likely warmer and wetter than it has been for most of its history." The chemistry of the meteorite, a type of coarse-grained rock called gabbro, shows that it experienced interactions with water when it was slowly cooling and crystallizing in the Martian subsurface. It was part of the Martian crust, the planet's outermost layer, but formed from magma originating at greater depths in the planet's mantle.

Mars is now cold, dry and desolate, but extensive evidence indicates it had water flowing on its surface in the form of rivers, lakes and an ocean in the northern hemisphere billions of years ago. Teghaza 001 was discovered in eight pieces, with the largest chunk about the size of a fist, in the desert roughly 21 miles (34 km) from the Malian village of Bir Chali. Its main minerals are feldspar and pyroxene, and it contains zircon crystals bearing the element uranium. The researchers ascertained its age using a technique based on the decay of uranium into lead over time. "Martian meteorites are our only samples from Mars, forming our basis for understanding the formation and differentiation of early Mars and allowing us to evaluate in laboratories whether ancient Mars could have supported habitable conditions," said Liu, lead author of a study on the meteorite published in the journal Science. "The detailed information we can extract from these meteorite samples complements and validates our exploration of Mars using satellites, landers and rovers," Liu said. This information provides clues about how the evolution of Mars diverged from Earth's when they were in their infancy and life was beginning to take hold on our planet, Liu said. Earth, Mars and the solar system's other planets formed roughly 4.5 billion years ago.     Only three Martian meteorites, including Teghaza 001, date to the planet's early history. One of them, discovered in Antarctica in 1984, was initially assessed as being about 4.5 billion years old but more recently was determined to have a similar age to Teghaza 001. Teghaza 001 likely is the older of the two, according to the new study. WATER WAS PERCOLATING Isotopes, or forms, of the elements oxygen and hydrogen present in the meteorite show that water was percolating down into the planet's deeper crust, as occurs on Earth, and mixing with molten rock from the mantle. "Multiple lines of evidence in Teghaza 001 suggest Mars' surface had water at more than 4.1 billion years ago. This is reflected by hydrogen isotopes in phosphate and oxygen isotopes in minerals and bulk samples," Liu said. Water is considered a key ingredient for life. "The findings lend support to the idea that early Mars had the necessary ingredients and conditions to harbor life, but do not directly answer the question of whether there was life on Mars," said planetary scientist and study co-author Lee Saper of NASA's Ames Research Center and the BAER Institute in California. "The rock is a snapshot in time that shows how a wetter early Mars with a thick atmosphere could have supported habitable conditions but that these conditions were waning rapidly over the first billion years or so of Mars' existence, trending towards its currently dry and inhospitable environment," Saper said. Teghaza 001's chemistry shows it is distinct from the other known Martian meteorites. It may have originated in the southern highlands, possibly from near Hellas Basin, one of the largest Martian impact craters, Liu said. The meteorite has a dramatic backstory. "It was blasted by an impact from the surface of Mars and was flying through space until its path crossed that of Earth. It then entered the atmosphere as a meteor and survived as a meteorite by landing in the Sahara," Liu said. "We do not know when the sample landed on Earth."

Shares of alternative asset managers rose on Thursday, with Blue Owl up 6.5 per cent and Ares Management gaining 2 per cent. THE GREAT AI BUILDOUT Data centers have become a critical part of the AI boom, housing the servers and computing equipment needed to train and run AI models. As the world's biggest technology companies race to expand computing capacity, demand for such facilities has surged, creating what industry executives have described as a generational opportunity for alternative asset managers. Blue Owl said it has more than 130 data centers operating or under construction, representing nearly 14 gigawatts of leased and owned capacity, with another 21 gigawatts in its pipeline. "We are not making a bet on AI when we invest in data centers," Blue Owl CFO Alan Kirshenbaum said, adding that the company does not expect demand for computing power to decline. "We are taking Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, credit risk." Ares Management said its data center development strategy focuses on metropolitan areas including Tokyo, Osaka, London and Sao Paulo, pre-leasing projects to investment-grade hyperscalers under 12- to 15-year leases with no termination rights and inflation escalators. Blackstone last week also highlighted its focus on physical infrastructure and long-term contracted assets. The vast majority of its data center portfolio has initial lease terms of 15 to 20 years, with 96 per cent of counterparties rated investment grade and an average market capitalisation of $2.5 trillion. "So when we think about risk, that doesn't feel particularly risky to us," Blackstone President Jonathan Gray told analysts on a post-earnings call. CAPEX BOOM The AI spending spree across data centers, power, equipment and software is one of the biggest investment waves in history, rivaling those that accompanied the advent of the internet and the expansion of railways. Ares estimates AI-related capex demand at just over $5 trillion through 2030, including roughly $2 trillion for physical data center buildings and adjacent power generation and transmission infrastructure. Asked about the AI selloff earlier this month, Ares CEO Michael Arougheti said investors were becoming more discerning about counterparty risk and how to price it. He also downplayed the impact of higher borrowing costs on AI capex financing, saying the alternative would be to fund projects with equity. "As the capex numbers have continued to scale, they went from largely equity-funded to then high-grade funded and now you're starting to see some of that funding demand flow through into the leveraged finance and private credit market. So there's an evolution here," Arougheti said. Ratings agency Moody's said earlier this week that AI and digital infrastructure were creating large, long-duration financing needs that broaden the private credit market beyond traditional direct lending. "Many borrowers and counterparties are investment grade. However, concentration, construction, residual-value and circular-financing risks are growing," Moody's said.

Markets will not be surprised by the announcement, but it will bring into focus the fact that the ECB is heading for a significant reshuffle in the first half of 2027, with Isabel Schnabel, Lagarde, and Philip Lane — the ECB’s de facto chief economist — all set to depart imminently." US INFLATION SPED UP US Commerce Department data showed that inflation accelerated in September as consumers paid more for gasoline and other goods, supporting economists' expectations of an interest rate increase from the Federal Reserve in December. The US economy, however, grew faster than expected in the third quarter, helped by resilient consumer spending and AI-driven business investment, data also showed. The dollar has not reacted significantly to the latest economic events largely because much of the data had been as expected and had already been priced in, said Eugene Epstein, head of structured products for Moneycorp North America. The dollar weakened 0.27 per cent to 0.826 against the Swiss franc. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said on Wednesday inflation can be lowered to the 2 per cent target without having to "throw sand in the gears" and slow growth or raise unemployment, pushing traders to rein in bets for rate hikes in 2027. Warsh also said the central bank would begin setting aside one of its eight regular policy meetings next year and two in 2028 to discuss major issues facing the institution and would not use them to consider changes in monetary policy. Still, markets are pricing in a nearly 80 per cent chance of a rate hike in December, according to the CME's FedWatch tool. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, fell 0.14 per cent to 101.98. The Japanese yen weakened 0.05 per cent against the greenback to 157.91 per dollar.   "A hold is widely expected at the BoJ's MPM this week," said Bank of America analysts led by Izumi Devalier in an investor note, referring to the bank's policy meeting. "While we do not expect the meeting to be market-moving for JPY, risks are skewed toward a higher JPY upon more than one hawkish dissent, given resilient underlying inflationary pressure." The New Zealand dollar was up 0.11 per cent at $0.56320, having slumped nearly 2 per cent following the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's surprise decision on Wednesday to keep rates at 2.75 per cent.

LONDON, Oct 29 : Major central banks took a break from interest rates rises this week, but they are by no means done, with energy prices near multi-month highs and no resolution to the conflict in the Middle East in sight. The Federal Reserve and European Central Bank both kept rates steady this week, but signaled with inflation above target they still have work to do. The ECB is also in focus as President Christine Lagarde announced she would step down early. The Bank of Japan is likely to stay on hold later this week, but next week's central bank meetings should see hikes, including from the Bank of England, its first of 2026. Here's where central banks in the Group of 10 developed economies stand, ranked from highest to lowest policy rate.

1/ AUSTRALIA The Reserve Bank of Australia has hiked interest rates four times this year. Their next policy decision is on November 3, and markets see a high chance of another hike, boosted by a hot inflation print and hawkish comments from governor Michele Bullock. 2/ NORWAY Norges Bank also meets next week after catching markets off guard with a hike in May and repeating the move in September, when it left the door open for additional tightening. Its annual core inflation held at 3.0 per cent in September, slightly above the central bank's 2.9 per cent forecast. 3/ UNITED STATES The Federal Reserve left rates unchanged on Wednesday ahead of next week's U.S. midterm elections while awaiting further evidence on inflation, which “remained elevated.” President Donald Trump has repeatedly called for rate cuts and recently accused policymakers of being "hostile" and "partisan" after September's rate increase. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh rejected those accusations, stressing the central bank's independence. Traders price 80 per cent chance of a hike in December and see at least one, likely two, further moves in 2027. 4/ BRITAIN The Bank of England has not raised rates this year so far, but that will likely change next week. Markets are almost fully pricing a hike, backed by recent data including hotter-than-expected September inflation and a pickup in wage growth. Governor Andrew Bailey has long warned the likelihood of a hike grows the longer energy prices stay high. 5/ NEW ZEALAND The Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised on Wednesday by keeping its benchmark official cash rate at 2.75 per cent in a narrow vote rather than hiking for the third time in a row. Governor Anna Breman said on Thursday chances the bank will hike the official cash rate in December are "high" Markets see roughly an 80 per cent probability of that. 6/ EURO AREA The European Central Bank delivered what market participants deem a hawkish hold, leaving rates unchanged but warning that inflation risks were rising. The central bank's most immediate challenge is the sharp rise in France's debt risk premium, driven by growing investor concerns over the country's debt burden and uncertain fiscal trajectory President Christine Lagarde resigned on Thursday so she could weigh in on political matters in France and globally. 7/ CANADA The Bank of Canada raised its key rate for the first time in more than three years on Wednesday, as widely expected, but Governor Tiff Macklem said policy remained slightly accommodative. The central bank hiked by 25 basis points to 2.5 per cent, still below the 2.75 per cent the BoC estimates is neither restrictive nor expansionary for the economy. The BoC also raised its inflation forecast for 2027 to 3.1 per cent from the 2.0 per cent predicted in July. 8/ SWEDEN Sweden's Riksbank, long in the dovish camp, now looks set for a rate hike, with markets pricing around an 80 per cent chance of one next week. Sweden's central bank chief earlier this month said that there was a strong case for a hike as the economy has been performing better than expected, and the risk of inflation overshooting its target has grown. 9/ JAPAN The Bank of Japan is set to keep rates steady this week. But, the central bank is expected to signal its readiness to keep raising borrowing costs, and sources told Reuters that it may also raise its inflation forecast. Recent data has pointed to broadening price pressures. Markets however aren't fully pricing in another hike from the BOJ until January 2027. 10/ SWITZERLAND The Swiss National Bank (SNB) is set to keep its policy rate at 0 per cent for the coming months. Minutes of its September meeting showed policymakers thought monetary conditions are "appropriate" to keep inflation within its target range over the medium term. Low yields should prevent the franc currency from appreciating too sharply, even though geopolitical tensions have often driven investors towards safe-haven assets in 2026.

Oct 29 : Alphabet is making billions of dollars selling homegrown AI chips it once reserved for internal use, but building inventory to meet surging demand is draining cash as the tech giant spends heavily on data centres. Unlike its traditional search and cloud businesses, selling AI chips that compete with Nvidia's requires Alphabet to spend on hardware well before customers pay, putting pressure on cash flow. The trade-off, outlined by finance chief Anat Ashkenazi on Alphabet's post-earnings call on Wednesday, offers an early look at the costs of a business that has emerged as one of the company's biggest growth areas as investors fret over AI's threat to its lucrative search advertising business. "Where previously inventory balances were primarily some of our hardware products, now those TPU (custom chip) systems that are not yet sold will be showing up. So you see cash going out ... it's not the traditional kind of capex but rather a different cycle of cash flow generation," Ashkenazi said.

HELSINKI, Oct 29 : Finnish police said on Thursday they had launched a criminal investigation into suspected breaches of environmental law at the construction site of a planned Google data centre in northern Finland. The project is part of a plan announced last month by Alphabet's Google to invest $15 billion in artificial intelligence infrastructure in Finland, which the US company described as its largest investment in Europe. Authorities have said Tuike Finland, a subsidiary of Alphabet's Google, conducted forest clearing and drainage at a planned site near the town of Muhos before the environmental impact assessments required under Finnish law had been completed. POLICE PROBE DRAINAGE AND WATER MANAGEMENT "We are investigating whether the company's operations have breached the water act and resulted in environmental damage," Detective Superintendent Kari Pakanen told Reuters, adding that a guilty finding could lead to a corporate fine. Pakanen declined to say whether any individuals could become a target of the investigation. Preliminary information showed ambiguities and shortcomings in the drainage and water management at Tuike's site, police said in a statement, adding that they would give an update in December but that the investigation would extend into 2027. On October 6, Finland's Supervisory Agency (LVV), which oversees environmental permits and assessments, ordered Google to halt preparatory measures altering the environment at Muhos as well as a separate site. It is up to regulator LVV to decide on any permits to restart the work at the data centre sites, Pakanen said. An LVV spokesperson said it was unclear how long it might take before the agency grants the relevant permits. "We've partnered closely with the government and communities in Finland on infrastructure for over a decade, and are actively responding to enquiries from LVV and other authorities," the Google spokesperson said. FINLAND'S APPEAL FOR DATA CENTRE INVESTMENT Finland's cool climate, low-carbon electricity and government endorsement of AI projects have contributed to making the country one of Europe's main destinations for data centre investments in recent years. Finland, similar in size to Germany but with a population of less than 6 million people, has had less vocal opposition to data centre buildouts than other places, including in the United States. AI data centres are among the main drivers of a projected rise of up to 40 per cent in Finland's electricity consumption in the coming years, if all agreed grid connection projects go ahead, grid operator Fingrid has said. Google's planned investments in Finland include data centres, electricity grid improvements and clean energy and battery projects to power services such as Gemini, Search, Maps and YouTube. Supporting Google's plan, Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo last month said that the deal would be a boost for the economy, playing down concerns it would suck up energy and push up power prices. The prime minister's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
